LONDON, England (CNN) -- When a woman dates a much older man, bystanders often speculate that she has only the most superficial of motives. French actress Ludivine Sagnier stars in veteran New Wave filmmaker Claude Chabrol's "The Girl Cut in Two." In "The Girl Cut in Two," veteran French filmmaker Claude Chabrol tells the story of one young woman for whom just the opposite is true. It stars French starlet Ludivine Sagnier as a young woman who rejects the amorous advances of a flashy, wealthy man her age, in favor of a sleazy affair with a fickle, 60 year-old father figure. Sagnier's desire to take on the role was also motivated by the allure of a much older man: Chabrol. "The idea of working with Claude Chabrol was the main attraction at the beginning," she told CNN. "He is a great French director, one of the pioneers of the French New Wave." "The guy has so much experience. I felt like I was a journalist, always asking things," continues Sagnier. "He's very old ... he's been through many, many things. This was his 66th movie, or something like that." Sagnier describes her character, Gabrielle de Neige, a charming, 20-something television weather girl, as "very naive." "She falls in a trap like a poor little lamb and she gets eaten by wolves. "The thing is, she doesn't have a dad, so she lacks affection, and sometimes that lack of affection can drive you to make mistakes. "I'd say I'm stronger than that," says 29 year-old Sagnier, who is perhaps best-known for her provocative portrayal of a highly-sexualized teenager opposite Charlotte Rampling in Francois Ozon's 2003 drama, "Swimming Pool." Sagnier who is often compared with screen sirens like Brigitte Bardot and Catherine Deneuve, drew international acclaim for a series of films in 2002 and 2003, but has recently has been taking smaller roles. Many of the qualities that attracted Sagnier to Chabrol are similar to those that draw her on-screen alter-ego Gabrielle to writer Charles Saint-Denis (Francois Berleand) -- Charles' knowledge of life, literature and his ability to treat her like a little girl, not as an equal. Sagnier says of working with Chabrol: "It was like opening a cinema book, because when you work with him he talks to you about Hitchcock, he talks to you about Kubrick. "He met everyone, so he's full of anecdotes, so you want to know more." Chabrol began his career in 1956, earning his stripes alongside fellow New Wave directors Jean-Luc Godard and Francois Truffaut. He became famous in the late 1960s for suspense thrillers such as "La Femme Infidele" (1969) and "Le Boucher" (1971). He has continued working prolifically in film and television ever since. Chabrol co-wrote the screenplay for the heartbreak drama, in which Sagnier character is consistently disappointed in love and let down by the men around her, with his step-daughter, Cecile Maistre, who also served as assistant director on the film. At the end of "The Girl Cut In Two," Sagnier appears on stage as a magician's assistant, smiling in the spotlight as she hears applause rise from the audience, the attention perhaps curing her depression over lovers lost. She lies in a box, appearing to be cut in half, the trick functioning as an almost literal embodiment of the film's title -- but clearly there's more to it than meets the eye. "She cuts into two men first of all, and she's also cut in two different sides of her personality," said Sagnier. "She has a part of shade and a part of lightness." Sagnier's fate since her collaboration with Chabrol has, thankfully, been a decidedly rosier affair: Since finishing "The Girl Cut in Two," she has starred in Jean-Francois Richet's, "Public Enemy No. 1," which received more nominations than any other film at the 2009 Cesar Awards, France's equivalent of the Oscars. The indefatigable Chabrol has recently wrapped up yet another film: "Bellamy" starring Gerard Depardieu. "The Girl Cut In Two" is released in the UK on 22 May 2009 .

LONDON, England (CNN) -- When a woman dates a much older man, onlookers often assume she is motivated by the most superficial of considerations. But in veteran French New Wave filmmaker Claude Chabrol’s “The Girl Cut in Two,” the opposite is true.

French starlet Ludivine Sagnier plays a young woman who rejects the amorous advances of a flashy, wealthy man her own age in favor of a sordid affair with a fickle, 60-year-old father figure.

Sagnier’s desire to take on the role was likewise inspired by the allure of a much older man: Chabrol.

“The idea of working with Claude Chabrol was the main attraction at the beginning,” she told CNN. “He is a great French director, one of the pioneers of the French New Wave.

“The guy has so much experience. I felt like I was a journalist, always asking things,” Sagnier continued. “He’s very old ... he’s been through many, many things. This was his 66th movie, or something like that.”

Sagnier describes her character, Gabrielle de Neige, a charming television weather presenter in her 20s, as “very naive.”

“She falls into a trap like a poor little lamb, and she gets eaten by wolves.

“The thing is, she doesn’t have a dad, so she lacks affection, and sometimes that lack of affection can drive you to make mistakes.

“I’d say I’m stronger than that,” said the 29-year-old Sagnier, who is perhaps best known for her provocative portrayal of a highly sexualized teenager opposite Charlotte Rampling in François Ozon’s 2003 drama “Swimming Pool.”

Sagnier, who is often compared with screen sirens such as Brigitte Bardot and Catherine Deneuve, earned international acclaim for a series of films in 2002 and 2003 but has recently been taking smaller roles.

Many of the qualities that attracted Sagnier to Chabrol resemble those that draw her on-screen alter ego, Gabrielle, to the writer Charles Saint-Denis (François Berléand): his knowledge of life and literature, and his ability to treat her like a little girl rather than as an equal.

Of working with Chabrol, Sagnier said: “It was like opening a cinema book, because when you work with him, he talks to you about Hitchcock, he talks to you about Kubrick.

“He met everyone, so he’s full of anecdotes, and you want to know more.”

Chabrol began his career in 1956, earning his stripes alongside fellow New Wave directors Jean-Luc Godard and François Truffaut. He became famous in the late 1960s for suspense thrillers such as “La Femme Infidèle” (1969) and “Le Boucher” (1971), and he has continued working prolifically in film and television ever since.

Chabrol co-wrote the screenplay for the heartbreak drama—in which Sagnier’s character is repeatedly disappointed in love and let down by the men around her—with his stepdaughter, Cécile Maistre, who also served as the film’s assistant director.

At the end of “The Girl Cut in Two,” Sagnier appears onstage as a magician’s assistant, smiling in the spotlight as applause rises from the audience, the attention perhaps easing her depression over lost lovers. She lies inside a box and appears to be cut in half, the trick serving as an almost literal embodiment of the film’s title—but clearly, there is more to it than meets the eye.

“She is torn between two men, first of all, and she is also divided between two different sides of her personality,” Sagnier said. “She has a part of shadow and a part of lightness.”

Thankfully, Sagnier’s fortunes since her collaboration with Chabrol have been decidedly brighter. Since completing “The Girl Cut in Two,” she has starred in Jean-François Richet’s “Public Enemy No. 1,” which received more nominations than any other film at the 2009 César Awards, France’s equivalent of the Oscars.

The indefatigable Chabrol has recently completed yet another film, “Bellamy,” starring Gérard Depardieu.

“The Girl Cut in Two” is released in the UK on May 22, 2009.

# Ludivine Sagnier steps into Claude Chabrol’s dangerous game in ‘The Girl Cut in Two’

**By CNN Entertainment**

Ludivine Sagnier’s luminous smile has rarely looked more precarious than it does in Claude Chabrol’s “The Girl Cut in Two.”

In the darkly comic 2007 drama, the French actress plays Gabrielle Deneige, an ambitious television weather presenter caught between two men: Charles Saint-Denis, a celebrated novelist old enough to be her father, and Paul Gaudens, the unstable heir to a pharmaceutical fortune.

“It’s a part where the character is constantly being watched and desired,” Sagnier said in interviews promoting the film. “But Gabrielle doesn’t immediately understand the danger she is in.”

That blindness is central to Chabrol’s design. Gabrielle believes she is choosing between romance and social advancement; the men around her treat her as an object in a contest of vanity, money and control. The film’s English title makes the metaphor explicit: She is divided not only between two suitors, but between innocence and experience, public image and private humiliation.

Sagnier said she was drawn to Gabrielle’s combination of confidence and vulnerability.

“She isn’t stupid,” the actress said. “She is young, and she wants to believe in what people tell her.”

For Sagnier, already known internationally for François Ozon’s “Swimming Pool” and “8 Women,” working with Chabrol meant entering the world of one of French cinema’s most prolific and mischievous filmmakers. She recalled accepting the opportunity enthusiastically, describing Chabrol’s set as relaxed even when the material turned cruel.

“Claude creates an atmosphere where you feel free,” she said. “He doesn’t make the psychology heavy. He lets the actors play.”

## A master of bourgeois unease

Chabrol, who died in 2010 at age 80, was one of the founding figures of the French New Wave. Like Jean-Luc Godard, François Truffaut, Éric Rohmer and Jacques Rivette, he began as a critic for the influential magazine *Cahiers du Cinéma* before moving behind the camera.

His 1958 debut, “Le Beau Serge,” is often cited as one of the first New Wave features. But while some of his contemporaries pursued increasingly radical forms, Chabrol developed a distinctive career inside recognizable genres—particularly thrillers, murder mysteries and domestic dramas.

Over more than five decades, he repeatedly turned his camera on comfortable French families whose polished manners concealed greed, resentment and violence. Films including “Les Biches,” “Le Boucher,” “La Cérémonie” and “Merci pour le Chocolat” earned him comparisons with Alfred Hitchcock, a filmmaker Chabrol studied and admired.

The resemblance was not simply a matter of suspense. Like Hitchcock, Chabrol had a taste for poisoned civility, morally compromised characters and humor that arrived at the least comfortable moment.

“The Girl Cut in Two,” loosely inspired by the early-20th-century scandal involving architect Stanford White, showgirl Evelyn Nesbit and millionaire Harry K. Thaw, gave Chabrol another opportunity to examine class and hypocrisy. He moved the story to contemporary Lyon and transformed it into a satire of celebrity, inherited wealth and male entitlement.

François Berléand plays Saint-Denis with cultivated self-satisfaction, while Benoît Magimel makes Paul both ridiculous and frightening. Between them stands Sagnier, whose bright television persona gradually gives way to shock and disillusionment.

Chabrol refuses to turn Gabrielle into a simple victim. She makes choices, misreads motives and participates in her own romantic fantasy. But the imbalance of power is unmistakable: Saint-Denis has age and cultural authority; Paul has money and family influence. Gabrielle’s supposed freedom exists largely on their terms.

That tension, Sagnier suggested, was what made the role compelling. Gabrielle’s journey is “a brutal loss of innocence,” she said, but also the beginning of a clearer understanding of the world around her.

In Chabrol’s cinema, clarity seldom brings comfort. By the time the illusion disappears, the damage has already been done—and the respectable people have resumed smiling.

That approach suits Gabrielle, a woman who initially appears confident and modern but is gradually divided between desire, social ambition and the demands of two possessive men. Loosely inspired by the early-20th-century American scandal involving architect Stanford White, showgirl Evelyn Nesbit and millionaire Harry Thaw, *The Girl Cut in Two* relocates the triangle to contemporary France. ### Ludivine Sagnier, Between Innocence and Experience

In Claude Chabrol’s *The Girl Cut in Two*, Ludivine Sagnier plays Gabrielle Deneige, a television weather presenter whose bright public image conceals a dangerous openness to reinvention. She is young, ambitious and accustomed to being watched—but not yet prepared for what it means to become the object of two men’s competing desires.

Sagnier approaches Gabrielle less as a naïve victim than as a woman testing the force of her own independence. Gabrielle enjoys attention and recognizes her appeal, yet she mistakes sophistication for emotional security. That confusion draws her toward Charles Saint-Denis, a celebrated writer decades her senior, played by François Berléand. Charles offers intellectual prestige, secrecy and the promise of initiation into an adult world. What he does not offer is equality.

The age difference is therefore more than a provocative romantic detail. It establishes an imbalance in experience and power. Charles can define the terms of the affair because he already knows its conventions: when to withdraw, what to conceal and how to separate desire from responsibility. Gabrielle enters the relationship believing intensity must imply significance. For Charles, intimacy can remain compartmentalized.

Sagnier’s performance preserves Gabrielle’s agency without disguising that imbalance. Her attraction to Charles is genuine; she is not simply coerced or deceived. But sincerity does not protect her from manipulation. Gabrielle’s willingness to follow him into increasingly private and troubling territory becomes part of Chabrol’s critique of a social world in which male privilege can masquerade as cultivation.

On the other side is Paul Gaudens, the unstable young pharmaceutical heir played by Benoît Magimel. If Charles possesses Gabrielle through secrecy and experience, Paul tries to possess her through marriage, money and jealousy. She is caught not only between an older man and a younger one, but between two systems of control: the libertine who refuses commitment and the bourgeois suitor who treats commitment as ownership.

That division gives the title *The Girl Cut in Two* its deepest resonance. It refers, first, to Gabrielle’s emotional split between Charles and Paul. It also suggests a fracture between her public and private selves, innocence and knowledge, autonomy and dependence. Even her name, “Deneige”—evoking snow—carries an ironic suggestion of purity onto which others project their fantasies.

Chabrol eventually turns the title into a visual joke through a stage illusion in which a woman appears to be sawed in half. Yet the trick sharpens the film’s cruelty: onstage, the divided woman emerges intact; in life, Gabrielle must survive damage that cannot be dismissed as illusion. Her final smile can be read as resilience, professionalism or another mask assumed for an audience.

Sagnier resists resolving that ambiguity. Gabrielle is neither destroyed nor simply liberated. She has learned how easily desire can be confused with power—and how performance can become a means of survival. The “girl” of the title is cut in two because the men around her insist on seeing only the version that satisfies them. Sagnier’s achievement is to let us glimpse the more complicated woman struggling to reassemble herself.

# Claude Chabrol’s ‘The Girl Cut in Two’ turns romance into a cruel illusion

**By CNN Arts & Culture**

Claude Chabrol spent much of his career looking beneath the polished surfaces of French bourgeois life. In “The Girl Cut in Two,” the veteran filmmaker found another deceptively elegant setting for obsession, class resentment and violence — and one of cinema’s most literal closing metaphors.

Released in France in 2007, the film stars Ludivine Sagnier as Gabrielle Deneige, an ambitious television weather presenter who becomes involved with Charles Saint-Denis, a celebrated writer played by François Berléand. Charles is older, married and practiced in the art of keeping desire separate from responsibility.

Gabrielle also attracts Paul Gaudens, portrayed by Benoît Magimel, the unstable heir to a pharmaceutical fortune. Caught between the two men, she is treated less as a person than as a prize: one wants to possess her in secret, the other in public.

Sagnier had already reached international audiences in François Ozon’s 2003 thriller “Swimming Pool,” in which she played the provocative Julie opposite Charlotte Rampling. That performance relied on ambiguity — Julie could seem carefree, calculating or almost unreal depending on who was watching. “The Girl Cut in Two” makes different use of Sagnier’s screen presence. Her Gabrielle begins as poised and optimistic, only to discover that charm and status offer little protection when powerful men decide the terms of her life.

The story was loosely inspired by the notorious 1906 killing of American architect Stanford White by millionaire Harry K. Thaw, whose wife, Evelyn Nesbit, had previously been involved with White. Chabrol and co-writer Cécile Maistre relocated the triangle to contemporary France, turning a historic scandal into a coolly observed study of celebrity, privilege and humiliation.

By then, Chabrol was one of the last active giants associated with the French New Wave. A former critic at *Cahiers du Cinéma*, he helped launch the movement with “Le Beau Serge” in 1958 and went on to direct films including “Les Cousins,” “Le Boucher” and “La Cérémonie.” Unlike some of his New Wave contemporaries, Chabrol often worked within recognizable genres, especially the thriller. But murder was rarely the whole subject. His deeper fascination was with the rituals and hypocrisies that make violence possible.

“The Girl Cut in Two” is characteristically controlled: drawing rooms, television studios and lavish parties become stages on which everyone performs a role. Its title refers to Gabrielle’s emotional division between Charles and Paul, but Chabrol saves its most striking interpretation for the final scene.

**Spoiler warning:** After betrayal, marriage and murder have torn Gabrielle’s life apart, she appears in a stage illusion performed by her magician uncle. Her body seems to be sliced in half. Moments later, she emerges intact, smiling for the audience.

The trick is both reassuring and deeply unsettling. Gabrielle has survived, but survival itself has become a performance. Chabrol shows the mechanism behind the illusion, then leaves viewers to wonder whether psychological wounds can be repaired as neatly as a magician’s box.

The film arrived late in both Chabrol’s career and a prolific period for Sagnier. She went on to appear in the “Mesrine” crime films, Alain Corneau’s “Love Crime,” the television series “The Young Pope” and François Ozon’s “The New Look,” among many other French and international projects.

Chabrol followed “The Girl Cut in Two” with “Bellamy,” starring Gérard Depardieu. Released in 2009, it became his final feature before his death in 2010 at age 80.

“The Girl Cut in Two” remains an apt late-career work: witty, poisonous and deceptively light on its feet. Like its closing illusion, the film invites applause for the spectacle while quietly asking viewers to consider the damage hidden inside the box.
